early-onset and later-onset schizophrenia are not phenotypally homogeneous, that there are clinical differences between them and that there are no differences in the prevalence of the most common delusional themes.

there were significant differences between early- and late-onset cases of schizophrenia in the prevalence of 11 of the 22 psychotic symptoms examined, and that these differences were not accounted for by the presence of other psychotic symptoms, or by age at onset, gender, social class, or marital status.
early-onset and later-onset schizophrenia are clinically different disorders, and the differences are not due to age-related changes in the prevalence of symptoms.

early- and late-onset forms of schizophrenia are different in terms of their symptomatology, but that the differences are not sufficient to warrant the conclusion that they are separate diseases.

the clinical features of early-onset schizophrenia are similar to those of late-onset schizophrenia, except for a number of symptoms that are more common in early onset, and for a few other symptoms that are more frequent in late-onset patients.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

early-onset schizophrenia is more likely to be characterised by positive symptoms, negative symptoms, and formal thought disorder, and late-onset cases are more likely to have persecutory delusions and third-person auditory hallucinations.

the clinical features of early- and late-onset cases are sufficiently similar for the disorders to share a common genetic basis, but sufficiently different to suggest that the disorders are not the same.

the clinical presentation of schizophrenia with early-onset is characterised by more prominent positive symptoms (e.g. formal thought disorder, delusions of passivity, grandiosity and thought insertion/withdrawal), whereas late-onset cases are characterised by more persecutory delusions, organised delusions and third-person, accusatory or abusive hallucinations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the clinical presentation of patients with early-onset and patients with late-onset schizophrenia are not similar and that the age of onset of illness is a useful clinical indicator for the presence of specific symptoms.
schizophrenia is not a homogeneous disease, and that there are different types of schizophrenia with different causes.
there is a need for more research to determine whether there are different genetic and environmental risk factors for schizophrenia with early and with late onset.
